newsitem.title: UK: Sterling steadies near three-week lows vs dollar.
newsitem.headline: Sterling steadies near three-week lows vs dollar.

text.p: Sterling steadied after crashing to a three-week low against the dollar and sliding against the mark early in Europe amid technical-driven trading.
The pound tumbled almost a percent against the dollar, with a major U.S. bank and a UK bank cited by traders as the key sellers who triggered the move.
Cable's slide gathered momentum after stop-loss orders to sell it were triggered about $1.6670, traders said.
"Loads of stops got quite heavily triggered on cable," said David Eddy, chief currency trader at Sumitomo Bank. "I am looking for it to go a bit lower to $1.6650."

Cable was at $1.6650/60 at 1050 GMT, up from a low at $1.6620 and compared to $1.6730/40 in late European trading on Thursday. Against the mark, sterling was at 3.0593/99 from 3.0625/35 late Thursday.

Cable's losses dragged sterling down as low as 3.0527 marks, almost two pfennigs from intraday highs. This has put expectations it would scale new peaks on dollar/mark's coat tails on the back burner for the time being.

Also, the Swiss franc's weakness yesterday and today has stirred some doubts about the extent of demand for currencies which are not expected to join European economic and monetary union, analysts said.
Expectations that EMU will be launched by a broad group of countries has undermined the mark against the currencies like the pound and the Swiss franc which are not involved in the project.
Sterling got little new impetus from the release of preliminary second-quarter gross domestic product figures, which were in line with economists' expectations.

The report kept expectations of higher UK interest rates alive, which will eventually help the pound clamber back towards the seven-and-a-half year high it set against the mark on Wednesday, traders said. Sterling could be in for a period of consolidation before then, though, they said.

"We should tread water around here for a while," said a trader at a German bank in London. "The market is speculating about when the next rate rise will be and how much it will be but that is not really an issue on a 24-hour horizon."
GDP rose 0.9 percent from the first quarter and was up 3.4 percent from a year ago. Excluding oil, the economy grew 1 percent from the previous quarter and 3.6 percent from a year earlier.
The data confirmed that UK domestic demand is strong enough to warrant higher interest rates, but failed to inject new enthusiasm into sterling bulls who had taken a beating earlier in Europe.
